1.text:
Same Disk, Different Worlds: Why?

Every planet in our solar system was built from the same spinning disk of gas and dust, about 4.6 billion years ago. Same ingredients, same kitchen. So why did the results turn out so different? Mercury is a cratered ball, Venus is an oven, Earth has oceans and life, and Mars is a cold desert.

That's the mystery for this deck, which wraps up the first quarter. Look at the four rocky planets on this page. They're drawn to scale, so you can see right away that size is one of the clues.

Here's the plan. First we find the three big patterns that decide a world's fate. Then we compare surfaces, then atmospheres, then water, and we ask why Earth is so special. Finally, you'll be the scientist and hunt for patterns in real NASA data.

Did you know? Venus and Earth are nearly twins in size, yet they ended up with completely different histories.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each.

I can explain how a world's size controls its inner heat and geologic activity. I can explain how distance from the Sun and the frost line set what planets are made of. I can connect fast spin and a molten core to magnetic fields and weather. I can build a flowchart from one disk to terrestrial and Jovian planets. I can compare impacts, volcanism, tectonics and erosion on different worlds.

I can also compare the air of Venus, Earth, Mars and Titan, using the ideas of outgassing, escape and greenhouse warming. I can describe water across the solar system and explain why Earth is unique. I can describe the habitable zone, a preview of a deck later this year. And I can graph NASA Fact Sheet data to find a pattern. A couple of these are enrichment goals, which means they're part of this course even if they aren't named in the standards.

3.text:
Same Disk, Different Worlds

Comparative planetology means comparing worlds side by side to find the patterns that shape them. It's like comparing siblings who grew up in the same house: the differences tell you something. Earth is our "control planet," the one we know best, so we compare everything else to it.

There are three big patterns. Size controls inner heat, volcanoes and plates. Distance from the Sun controls temperature, and whether a world is built of rock or ice. Rotation, or spin, helps decide magnetic fields and weather.

The differences between worlds follow these patterns. They aren't random. And notice that distance isn't the only thing that matters. Venus and Earth sit at similar distances from the Sun but have very different surfaces and air.

4.text:
Size Sets the Inner Heat

A rocky world starts out hot. Its internal heat is heat left over from formation plus heat from radioactive decay. That heat slowly leaks out through the surface, and once it's gone, the world goes quiet. Sunlight only warms the surface; it isn't what keeps a planet's insides hot.

The pattern: the bigger the world, the longer it stays hot. Think of a baked potato and a tater tot fresh out of the oven. The tiny one cools much faster. A small world has a lot of surface area for its volume, so heat escapes quickly. A big world also holds more radioactive material, so it makes more heat.

Look at the three worlds, drawn to scale. The Moon, the smallest, has cooled and been quiet for billions of years. Most of its eruptions ended about 3 billion years ago, with small ones until about 1 to 2 billion years ago. Mars is in the middle: partly cooled, with a few volcanoes. Earth, the largest, is still hot inside, with volcanoes and moving plates.

Did you know? Size is a strong rule of thumb, not a law. Jupiter's moon Io is small, but Jupiter's tides heat it so much that it's covered in volcanoes.

5.text:
Distance Sets the Temperature

Distance from the Sun is the second pattern. In the young solar system, the inner part of the disk was hot. It was too warm there for water and other ices to freeze, so only rock and metal could become solid.

Farther out was a boundary called the frost line: the distance from the young Sun beyond which ices could form. Beyond it, worlds could collect rock, metal and ice. With all that extra material, they grew big enough to pull in huge amounts of gas. For a star like the Sun, the frost line sat at about 2.7 AU, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It wasn't a wall of ice, just a temperature boundary.

That's why the planets come in two groups. Inside the frost line are the terrestrial planets: closer, hotter, rocky and small. Outside are the Jovian planets: farther, colder, icy and giant. The picture on this slide isn't to scale.

Did you know? Distance still sets temperature today. Every planet gets colder the farther it is from the Sun, except one. You'll find out which on Slide 15.

6.text:
Spin Shapes Fields & Weather

The third pattern is rotation, and it teams up with what's inside a planet. Earth has a fast spin plus a molten nickel-iron core, and together they give it a magnetic field. The solar wind squishes that field into a teardrop shape around us.

Now meet Venus. It takes 243 days to spin once, and it spins backward! Venus is about Earth's size with a similar iron core, but it has no global magnetic field. Its day is even longer than its 224.7-day year. Spin isn't everything, though. Mars spins in 24.6 hours, almost like Earth, but its core has cooled, so it has no global field today.

Spin shapes weather too. Jupiter has a 10-hour spin, the shortest day of any planet. That fast spin drives strong jet streams that stretch its clouds into dark belts and bright zones.

Did you know? Mercury spins slowly, once every 59 Earth days, yet it still has a weak magnetic field, about 1% as strong as Earth's.

7.text:
Model It: One Disk, Many Worlds

Now you're the model builder. Your job is a flowchart that takes the solar system from a cloud of gas all the way to planets.

Here are the steps. 1. A cloud collapses under its own gravity, and the young Sun forms in the hot center. 2. The rest spins faster and flattens into a spinning disk. 3. Grains collide and stick together, building planetesimals about a kilometer to many kilometers across. Then the path splits. 4a. Inside the frost line, you get terrestrial planets. 4b. Beyond the frost line, you get Jovian planets. 4c. Leftovers become moons, asteroids and comets.

Draw each step and add a caption. Then mark where the frost line goes, and write one reason the inner and outer planets differ.

Did you know? The planets didn't form one at a time in order from the Sun. They all grew at the same time across the disk.

8.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Let's test those three patterns. Why is Mars geologically quieter than Earth?

Is it A) it is smaller, so it lost its inner heat faster, B) it is farther away, so the Sun can't heat its core, C) it spins much more slowly than Earth, or D) it formed from different material? Think about where a planet's inner heat comes from, and check the spin numbers on Slide 6. Choose one and explain why the others miss.

9.text:
Four Ways to Shape a Surface

Four processes shape every solid surface in the solar system. The first is impacts: craters from space rocks, which you see all over the Moon and Mercury. The second is volcanism: molten rock erupting from inside, on Io, Venus, Mars and Earth.

The third is tectonics: the stretching, squeezing or moving of a surface by forces from inside. Earth's moving plates are the big example. The fourth is erosion, which wears surfaces down: water and wind on Earth, and even methane rivers on Saturn's moon Titan.

Here's the pattern. Impacts happen everywhere. But the other three need energy from inside, or an atmosphere with liquids. So big worlds, and worlds with air, erase their craters the fastest.

Did you know? Erosion doesn't need water. Wind wears down rock on Mars, and liquid methane carves channels on Titan.

10.text:
Count Craters, Read the Age

Crater counting works like a clock. Space rocks hit every world, so the longer a surface sits there, the more craters it collects. More craters on a surface means an older surface. Few craters means something erased the old ones not long ago.

Compare three worlds, from older to younger. On the Moon, the big eruptions ended about 3 billion years ago, so most of its surface keeps every crater. On Venus, most of the surface is under 500 million years old. On Earth, the seafloor, about two-thirds of the surface, is under 200 million years old, because plate tectonics keeps reworking it.

Big, active worlds erase their craters. Io is the extreme case: its volcanoes cover craters faster than space rocks can make them, so it has no large craters at all.

Did you know? A young surface doesn't mean a young world. Earth's surface is young, but Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old.

11.text:
Bright Rays = Young Crater

Some craters have bright lines splashing out from them, like spokes on a wheel. Those are rays, made of rock thrown out by the impact.

Over time, radiation and tiny impacts slowly darken a surface. That's called space weathering. Fresh rays show lighter rock that hasn't been darkened yet. So bright rays mean a crater is young, and a gray, faded crater is old.

12.text:
The Biggest Volcano Is on Mars

Mars is a small planet, yet it has the biggest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons. It rises about 22 km above Mars's average surface level. Compare that to Mount Everest at 8.8 km. Olympus Mons is about 2.5 times taller! On the drawing, heights are to scale, but widths are squeezed. The real volcano is a broad shield about 600 km across, not a pointy peak.

How can a smaller planet build a bigger volcano? Two reasons. Mars has less gravity, and it has no moving plates. On Earth, a plate slides over a hot spot, so instead of one giant volcano we get a chain of them, like the Hawaiian Islands. On Mars the crust stays put, so one volcano keeps growing and growing.

Did you know? You might see 26 km listed for Olympus Mons. That number is measured from the low plains at its base. Measured from Mars's average surface level, it's about 22 km.

13.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Imagine a spacecraft photographs a world with very few craters. What is the best conclusion?

Is it A) its surface was renewed recently, B) it has never been hit by anything, C) it is far from the asteroid belt, or D) it is a very small, cold world? Use what you learned about crater counting and the size pattern. Pick your answer and explain how the Moon and Earth help you rule out the others.

14.text:
Where Air Comes From

Planets weren't born with the air they have now. Their atmospheres were built over time. The main way is outgassing: gas released from a planet's interior, mostly through volcanoes. Magma holds dissolved gases, and as it rises and the pressure drops, those gases escape into the air, a bit like the fizz rushing out of a soda when you open it.

What comes out? Water vapor (H2O) is the most common volcanic gas, followed by carbon dioxide (CO2) and sulfur dioxide (SO2). Icy impacts add gas too, when comets and icy asteroids crash in and deliver water and other ingredients.

Remember the size pattern? Volcanoes need inner heat, so big, hot worlds keep outgassing longest. Tiny Mercury was too small and hot to keep its gas.

Did you know? Earth's oxygen didn't come from volcanoes. It came much later, from living things.

15.text:
Venus: A Greenhouse Gone Runaway

Venus has an average surface temperature of 464 °C. That's hot enough to melt lead. And here's the odd part: Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury, yet hotter. Line up the planets on the thermometer: Mercury 167 °C, Venus 464 °C, Earth 15 °C, Mars -65 °C.

The culprit is the greenhouse effect. Gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor let sunlight in but trap the heat the surface gives off, like a car sitting in the sun with the windows rolled up. Venus has a crushing atmosphere, 92 times the pressure of Earth's and 96.5% CO2. It traps so much heat that the greenhouse ran away. Venus is about 510 degrees hotter than it would be with no greenhouse gases.

Earth's greenhouse effect is gentle, and we need it. Without it, Earth would average about -19 °C instead of 15 °C. Venus went too far and lost its water for good. Mars went the other way: it lost the CO2 it needed to stay warm, and its water froze.

Did you know? The Sun is about 30% brighter now than when it formed, and it keeps slowly brightening.

16.text:
Losing Air to Space

Planets can lose air as well as gain it. Atmospheric escape is gas lost from the top of an atmosphere into space. Two big threats are on this slide: the solar wind, and weak gravity that can't hold gas down.

Earth has a magnetic field that turns the solar wind aside, protecting our air. Mars has no global field, so the solar wind reaches its upper atmosphere and the gas is stripped away. NASA's MAVEN mission measured Mars losing about 100 grams of gas every second today, and much faster during solar storms. Over billions of years, that slow leak helped turn a warmer, wetter Mars into the cold, dry planet we see now.

A magnetic field isn't the only shield, though. Gravity matters too. Venus has no magnetic field of its own, but it's big enough to hold on to its thick air.

Did you know? Venus has about 100 times more "heavy hydrogen" (deuterium) compared with regular hydrogen than Earth does. That's evidence it once had much more water and lost the lighter hydrogen to space.

17.text:
Hot and Light Escape First

Gas molecules are always zooming around. Light, hot gas moves fast. If a molecule moves faster than a planet's escape speed, it can leak away into space.

That's why small worlds lose their lightest gases, hydrogen and helium, first. Heavier gases move more slowly and are easier to keep. Mars held on to CO2, the heaviest of its common gases.

Big planets have much higher escape speeds. Jupiter's is the highest of all, so the giant planets kept the hydrogen and helium they collected when they formed.

18.text:
Titan: A Moon With Thick Air

Most moons have no air at all. Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is different. It has 45% more air pressure at its surface than Earth has. Standing there would feel like being about 4.5 m underwater in a pool. Like Earth's air, Titan's is mostly nitrogen (N2), with a little methane (CH4).

Titan is the only world besides Earth with liquid on its surface. It has methane rain, rivers, lakes and seas, a whole liquid cycle like our water cycle, just with a different liquid. And it's cold: -179 °C. At that temperature, water ice acts like rock.

Sunlight keeps breaking down Titan's methane, so something must keep refilling it. Where that methane comes from is still a mystery.

Did you know? NASA's Titan page says the pressure is about 60% more than Earth's, but the Huygens probe measured about 45% when it landed in 2005. When numbers disagree, go back to the original measurement.

19.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Venus and Earth are about the same size. So why is Venus so much hotter?

Is it A) its thick CO2 air traps heat: a runaway greenhouse, B) it is closer to the Sun than Mercury, C) its slow spin bakes one side, or D) its volcanoes heat the surface directly? Look back at the thermometer on Slide 15 and the distances you know. Choose an answer and be ready to defend it.

20.text:
Water Across the Solar System

Water is common in the solar system, but liquid water on a surface is rare. Let's take a tour. Venus lost its water to space. Earth has liquid oceans on the surface. Mars has ice under the poles and old riverbeds that show water once flowed there.

Now look at the icy moons. Many of them have a subsurface ocean: liquid water hidden beneath an icy crust. Jupiter's moon Europa has a salty ocean under the ice, maybe holding about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans. Saturn's moon Enceladus has jets that spray its ocean into space, where spacecraft can sample it. And Titan likely has a water ocean under its ice, even though its surface lakes are methane.

Notice what's going on. Beyond the frost line, water is everywhere, but frozen. These hidden oceans stay liquid because of heat from inside the moons. Sizes on the slide are not to scale.

21.text:
Why Earth Is Unique

71% of Earth's surface is ocean. Earth is the only planet with surface liquid water, and the only place known with life. Life got its start in those oceans about 3.8 billion years ago.

Why Earth, and not Venus or Mars? Earth combines all three patterns from Part 1. Thanks to its size, it's still hot inside, so moving plates recycle the crust. Thanks to its spin and molten core, a magnetic field shields the air. And it has the right distance and size to keep liquid water, with a greenhouse effect that's just strong enough.

Earth's air is also unusual. Venus and Mars are both about 96% CO2. Earth is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, because water and then life changed it.

Did you know? Earth isn't the biggest planet. It's only the fifth largest. Size alone doesn't make it special.

22.text:
Preview: The Habitable Zone

The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. Some people call it the "Goldilocks zone": not too hot, not too cold.

For our Sun, the zone runs from about 0.99 AU to 1.70 AU. Closer than that is too hot, and farther is too cold. Venus, at 0.72 AU, sits in the too-hot region. Earth is just right, near the inner edge. Mars, at 1.52 AU, is actually inside the zone too, which sets up a puzzle on Slide 23. The band on the slide is drawn to scale in AU, but the planet sizes are not.

Every star has a habitable zone, but where it sits depends on how bright the star is. You'll come back to this idea later in the year when we hunt for planets around other stars.

Did you know? As the Sun slowly brightens, its habitable zone creeps outward over time.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Here's a puzzle. Mars sits inside the Sun's habitable zone. So why is there no liquid water on its surface?

Is it A) its air is too thin for liquid water to last, B) it is outside the habitable zone, C) Mars never had any water, or D) Mars is too hot for liquid water? Use what you learned about Mars's air on Slide 16 and the water tour on Slide 20. Pick one and explain.

24.text:
Data Activity: The Fact Sheet

Time to work like a planetary scientist. This table comes from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, with a surface-activity column from the OpenStax astronomy textbook. Distances are in millions of km.

Read across the rows. Mercury: 4,879 km wide, 57.9 million km from the Sun, 167 °C, a 1,407.6-hour spin, a magnetic field, very low activity. Venus: 12,104 km, 108.2, 464 °C, -5,832.5 hours, no field, high activity. Earth: 12,756 km, 149.6, 15 °C, 23.9 hours, a field, high activity. The Moon: 3,475 km, orbits Earth, -20 °C, 655.7 hours, no field, no activity. Mars: 6,792 km, 228.0, -65 °C, 24.6 hours, no field, low activity.

The giants have no solid surface, but they all have magnetic fields. Jupiter: 142,984 km, 778.5, -110 °C, 9.9 hours. Saturn: 120,536 km, 1,432.0, -140 °C, 10.7 hours. Uranus: 51,118 km, 2,867.0, -195 °C, -17.2 hours. Neptune: 49,528 km, 4,515.0, -200 °C, 16.1 hours. A negative rotation means the planet spins backward. Pick two columns, graph them on the next slide, and find the pattern.

Did you know? Jupiter is the biggest planet but has the shortest day, just 9.9 hours.

25.text:
Graph It: Find the Pattern

Now turn numbers into a picture. For Graph A, plot distance from the Sun (millions of km) on the x-axis and mean temperature (°C) on the y-axis. Because the giants are so far out, you can plot the rocky planets only, or use a scale break on your axis.

For Graph B, plot diameter (km) on the x-axis and surface activity on the y-axis, for the solid worlds. Put activity in order from none to high.

Look closely at your graphs. Which world breaks a pattern? Use what you learned about size and heat on Slide 4 and Venus's atmosphere on Slide 15 to explain why. Remember, a point that doesn't fit isn't a mistake. It's a clue.

26.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 5

Use your Graph A. Which world breaks the pattern "farther from the Sun, colder"?

Is it A) Venus, B) Mercury, C) Mars, or D) Neptune? Find the point that sits far off the trend line. Choose your answer and explain what causes it.

27.text:
Exit Ticket

You compared a whole family of worlds today. Show what you've learned with three questions.

First, name the three patterns (size, distance, spin) and one effect of each. Second, Venus, Earth and Mars started alike. Why did their air end up so different? Third, why can Earth keep liquid water on its surface when Mars cannot?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

28.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus. Picture a small, warm planet. Which escapes first, hydrogen or carbon dioxide? Why?

Think about Slide 17: how mass and temperature change how fast a gas molecule moves.

29.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.1: build a flowchart, with diagrams and descriptions, of how the solar system formed from a cloud of gas and dust. Include the star, planetesimals, protoplanets, rocky and giant planets, moons and small bodies. Your flowchart task was Slide 7. ES.2.2: describe the different kinds of objects in the solar system, know that planets have been found around other stars and even drifting with no star, and describe how our solar system is organized. The data activity on Slides 24 and 25 practiced this.

ES.6.2: explain how Earth's liquid outer core makes the magnetosphere, and how it protects people and satellites from the solar wind. This deck only previews that idea. You'll learn it in full in Deck 11.
